slides.title: Tip 1 — Use Setting Description on an As-Needed Basis
Tip 2 — Sometimes Tell How Characters Feel
Writing Tips for Aphants
slides.question: What is Zarins' first tip for writers who want to reach readers with aphantasia?

options.text: Avoid all description of settings and landscapes.
options.explanation: She says 'on an as-needed basis', not to avoid it entirely.

options.text: Use setting description on an as-needed basis, delivering sensory details like breadcrumbs one at a time.
options.explanation: She says aphants digest sensory information best when it is delivered like breadcrumbs, one situated detail at a time.

options.text: Use more visual similes and metaphors.
options.explanation: That might help sighted readers but not aphants who cannot visualize.

slides.title: Word Card
slides.translation: The inability to visualize images in the mind's eye; also called 'mind blindness'
slides.context: Term coined in 2015 by Adam Zeman. About 2% of people have aphantasia.
slides.example: I'm an aphant — someone with aphantasia, the condition of lacking a mind's eye and the ability to visualize.

slides.title: Word Card
slides.translation: Having a brain that processes information in atypical ways (e.g., autism, aphantasia, synesthesia)
slides.context: Used to describe the population of readers who experience fiction differently due to neurological conditions.
slides.example: Diverse perspectives in speculative fiction are increasingly represented, including neurological diversity such as autism or synesthesia.

slides.title: Word Card
slides.translation: Fiction that imagines alternative realities, including science fiction, fantasy, and related genres
slides.context: The genre most relevant to aphant readers because it demands visualization.
slides.example: Speculative fiction helps people speculate — and it also helps us feel things, sometimes deeply.
